content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed an operational handbook on tuberculosis (TB) treatment, specifically focusing on drug-resistant TB. This handbook is designed to provide practical guidance to complement the WHO consolidated guidelines on TB treatment, including multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) and isoniazid-resistant TB (Hr-TB). The document outlines the selection and design of treatment regimens for these conditions, based on the latest WHO recommendations formulated using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. Drug susceptibility testing (DST) is a critical component of TB management. It involves in vitro testing using molecular or genotypic techniques to detect resistance-conferring mutations or phenotypic methods to determine susceptibility to specific medications. Isoniazid-resistant TB (Hr-TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains resistant to isoniazid but susceptible to rifampicin. Rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) is caused by strains resistant to rifampicin, which may also exhibit resistance to other first-line or second-line TB drugs. Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) is defined as resistance to at least both isoniazid and rifampicin. The term MDR/RR-TB is used to collectively describe cases of MDR-TB and RR-TB, as both are eligible for treatment with MDR-TB regimens. MDR/RR-TB treatment refers to therapeutic options for patients with these forms of TB. Extensive or advanced TB disease is characterized by bilateral cavitary disease or extensive parenchymal damage on chest radiography. In children under 15 years, advanced disease is typically defined by the presence of cavities or bilateral disease on chest radiography. Severe extrapulmonary TB includes conditions such as miliary TB or TB meningitis. The definition of extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) is evolving due to the phasing out of injectable drugs, the emergence of resistance patterns relevant to current and future regimens, and advances in diagnostic methods and DST. Future expert consultations will address changes to the XDR-TB definition, which will be reflected in revised WHO surveillance and reporting guidelines. The selection of appropriate regimens for patients with MDR-TB strains exhibiting additional resistance to fluoroquinolones (pre-XDR) is becoming increasingly feasible due to rapid advances in molecular DST. Second-line TB medications are used for the treatment of drug-resistant TB. Some first-line drugs, such as ethambutol, isoniazid, and pyrazinamide, may also be included in MDR-TB regimens. Streptomycin is now considered a second-line TB drug and is used only as a substitute for amikacin when amikacin is unavailable, or when there is confirmed resistance to amikacin but susceptibility to streptomycin, and when an all-oral regimen cannot be constituted. Shorter MDR-TB regimens last less than 12 months and are largely standardized. Longer MDR-TB regimens last at least 18 months and are designed using a hierarchy of recommended medicines to include a minimum number of effective TB drugs based on drug-resistance patterns or patient history. Empiric treatment refers to the initiation of therapy before laboratory confirmation of the drug-resistance pattern. The availability of rapid molecular testing facilitates the initiation of definitive regimens with a high probability of cure. Off-label use refers to the use of a pharmaceutical agent for an indication, age group, dosage, duration, or route of administration that differs from what was approved by a national drug regulatory authority. Certain drugs, such as fluoroquinolones, clofazimine, and linezolid, have been used off-label for MDR-TB treatment. However, sufficient evidence on their efficacy and safety in TB treatment has rendered their current use no longer considered off-label. The decision to use drugs off-label is typically based on clinical judgment, aiming to provide better treatment outcomes for patients. This has been observed with the use of bedaquiline or delamanid beyond six months. An adverse event is any untoward medical occurrence in a TB patient during treatment with a pharmaceutical product, which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the treatment. A serious adverse event is one that results in death, a life-threatening experience, hospitalization or prolonged hospitalization, persistent or significant disability, or a congenital anomaly. Serious adverse events that require intervention to prevent such outcomes are also included. The WHO operational handbook provides detailed guidance on the management of drug-resistant TB, including the use of diagnostic tools, treatment regimens, and monitoring strategies, to ensure effective and safe care for patients.
